title: Anna Karenina
author: Leo Tolstoy
openingChapterLabel: Part I, Chapter 1 — The Oblonsky household
openingText: All happy families are alike; each unhappy family is unhappy in its own way.
about:
Anna Karenina follows intertwined stories of love, family and the search for a meaningful life. Anna comes to Moscow to help her brother Stiva and his wife Dolly after his infidelity. There she meets Count Vronsky. Meanwhile, the landowner Konstantin Levin hopes to marry Dolly’s younger sister Kitty. The novel moves between these households, city society and country work, allowing different characters to experience the same events very differently.

Tolstoy worked on the novel from 1873 to 1877. The first seven parts appeared in The Russian Messenger in 1875–1877. A disagreement with its editor over the final part’s treatment of Russian volunteers supporting Serbia led to Part Eight appearing separately in 1877. The first complete book edition followed in 1878.

Read the social scenes as closely as the dramatic ones: a glance, an invitation, a missed visit or a change of address can alter a relationship. Levin’s questions about work, faith and responsibility belong to the same novel as Anna’s story. Neither strand can be reduced to a simple lesson about who deserves happiness.

angleCards.title: Anna and her society
angleCards.text: Follow how Anna’s relationships change as private feelings become public knowledge. Notice the different freedoms granted to men and women.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow Anna’s choices, attachments and isolation, while distinguishing other characters’ judgments from the narrator’s.

angleCards.title: Levin’s questions
angleCards.text: Levin seeks a meaningful way to live through farming, family, reading and faith. Watch how practical life complicates his theories.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to track what Levin learns from work, love and other people, and what his final insight does and does not resolve.

angleCards.title: Three households
angleCards.text: Compare the Oblonskys, the Karenins and the family Levin and Kitty build. Money, children, work and social expectations shape each household.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to compare the three families without assuming that one supplies a simple model for the others.

angleCards.title: Names and voices
angleCards.text: A person may appear under a first name, patronymic, surname or affectionate nickname. Stiva is Stepan; Dolly is Darya; Kitty is Ekaterina; Kostya is Konstantin; Seryozha is Sergey.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow changing forms of address and notice whose perceptions shape each scene.

cast.name: Anna Arkadyevna Karenina
cast.description: Stiva’s sister, Karenin’s wife and Seryozha’s mother. Her visit to Moscow brings her into Vronsky’s orbit. Her intelligence and social confidence coexist with needs and fears that others often fail to understand.

cast.name: Count Alexey Kirillovich Vronsky
cast.description: A wealthy cavalry officer who attracts Kitty’s hopes before falling in love with Anna. His ambitions, friendships and sense of honor do not always fit the life Anna needs.

cast.name: Alexey Alexandrovitch Karenin
cast.description: Anna’s older husband, a senior government official. His concern for duty, reputation and religious obligation intersects with genuine suffering and moments of compassion.

cast.name: Konstantin Dmitrievitch Levin
cast.description: A landowner concerned with farming, family and the purpose of life. His brothers Nikolay and Sergey Ivanovitch reveal different possibilities for living and thinking.

cast.name: Princess Ekaterina “Kitty” Shtcherbatskaya
cast.description: Dolly’s younger sister. Her disappointment, recovery and growing confidence form a story of their own. Her practical care repeatedly challenges Levin’s assumptions.

cast.name: Prince Stepan “Stiva” Arkadyevitch Oblonsky
cast.description: Anna’s brother and Dolly’s husband. Charming and sociable, he often leaves others to bear the cost of his appetites and financial choices.

cast.name: Darya “Dolly” Alexandrovna Oblonskaya
cast.description: Stiva’s wife and Kitty’s elder sister. Childcare, money and her husband’s infidelity shape her daily life. Her visits and conversations connect the novel’s households.

whyItMatters.title: A question about families
whyItMatters.body: The opening claim about happy and unhappy families invites testing against the lives that follow. Love does not remove the pressure of money, children, habits or unequal expectations. Notice how a household looks different from inside each person’s experience.

whyItMatters.title: A changing society
whyItMatters.body: The novel places intimate decisions alongside farming, provincial elections, government jobs and debate about war. The final discussions concern volunteers supporting Serbia against the Ottoman Empire. Speakers disagree about compassion, nationalism, public opinion and the right to make war; their arguments are not interchangeable with an editorial verdict.

whyItMatters.title: Meaning in ordinary life
whyItMatters.body: Levin’s reflections grow from experiences that thinking alone cannot settle: illness, marriage, childbirth, work and fear for those he loves. His concluding insight does not make him instantly patient or free of doubt. Read the ordinary conversation around it alongside the reflection itself.
